C>\frac{A^2T^5}{S^2},\qquad

Put
\[
 \mathcal Q=\frac{|(a-b)(a-s)(b-s)|}{BS^2},\qquad
 c_*=\frac{9999}{10000}\left(\frac{200}{19}\right)^2.
\]
The retained inequality and \(T>2ABS\) yield
\[
 C>32c_*\left(\frac1{\mathcal Q}-\frac{\mu}{A^2B^2}\right)^2
                         A^7B^5S^3.
\]
Since \(A^2B^2\ge81\) and \(0<\mathcal Q\le8\),
\[
 32c_*\left(1-\frac{8\mu}{81}\right)^2
 =\frac{5468347165039}{1582031250}>3456.
\]
Consequently, with \(K=54\) and \(\beta=3456\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-gap}
 C>K A^7B^5S^3,\qquad
 C>\frac{\beta}{\mathcal Q^2}A^7B^5S^3.
\end{equation}
The second estimate will be retained at one junction.

\paragraph{A bound for $\mathcal Q^2\Phi$.}
Write \(u=A/B,\ v=B/S,\ w=|b-s|/S\), and
\(\Phi=\max(w^6,vw^5)\). The identities
\[
 (a-b)(a-s)=a^2-a(b+s)+bs,\qquad
 |b+s|^2=2B^2+2S^2-|b-s|^2
\]
give
\[
 \mathcal Q\le w[1+u^2v+u\sqrt{2+2v^2-w^2}]
 \le w[2+\sqrt{4-w^2}].
\]
If \(w\ge v\), substitute \(x=\sqrt{4-w^2}\) to obtain
\[
 \mathcal Q^2\Phi\le(2-x)^4(2+x)^6
 \le F:=\left(\frac85\right)^4\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)^6.
\]
Indeed the logarithmic derivative on \((0,2)\) has the sign of
\(4-10x\), so the maximum occurs at \(x=2/5\).
If \(w<v\le1\), then \(\mathcal Q\le4w\) and
\(\mathcal Q^2\Phi\le16vw^7\le16<F\).
Thus the same bound holds in every case.

There are two choices of matrices. The universal matrix consists of
the six rows
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ff-p0rows}
 R_{ab},R_{bs},R_{as},T_{ab},T_{bs},T_{sa}.
\end{equation}
In columns $(Q_0,Q_a,Q_b,Q_s)$, the determinant of its first three
rows and $T_{ab}$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ff-p0det}
 15750a^2b^2s^2(a-b)^4(a-s)(b-s)F_s,
 \quad F_s=7(2s-a-b)+6c[3s^2-(a+b)s-ab].
\end{equation}
The alternative four-row matrix is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ff-prows}
 R_{ab},\quad H=R_{ab}+R_{bs}-R_{as},\quad
 T_{ab},\quad V=T_{as}-T_{bs};
\end{equation}
its determinant is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ff-pdet}
 -78750a^2b^2s^2(a-b)^5(a-s)(b-s)F_s.
\end{equation}
Both identities are checked from the printed rows by expanding only
the constant and linear coefficients in $c$. Replacement of the column indexed by $0$ by its $O(c^{-5})$ residual makes their determinant degree at
most $2+2+2-5=1$. Thus this finite expansion verifies the complete
identities, with no unspecified higher coefficients.

The universal matrix always has rank four. Its cyclic minors have
the nonzero products displayed in \eqref{eq:ff-p0det}
times $F_a,F_b,F_s$, up to signs. With
$\sigma_1=a+b+s$, $\sigma_2=ab+as+bs$, these factors are
\[
 F_x=7(3x-\sigma_1)+6c(3x^2-\sigma_2).
\]
If all three vanished, subtracting the equations for $s,b$ and $s,a$
would give $7+6c(s+b)=7+6c(s+a)=0$, contrary to $c\ne0$ and $a\ne b$.
For the four-row matrix it suffices to prove $F_s\ne0$.
If $S\ge2B$, then
\[
 |3s^2-(a+b)s-ab|\ge\tfrac74S^2,\qquad |2s-a-b|\le3S,
\]
so the $c$ term dominates under \eqref{eq:ff-pguards}.
Alternatively, if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ff-allSrank}
 B\ge qA,\qquad q\ge18/17,\qquad S\ge3,
\end{equation}
then for every $S\ge B$,
\[
 |3s^2-(a+b)s-ab|\ge(2-2/q)S^2,
 \qquad |2s-a-b|\le(3+1/q)S.
\]
Indeed $6C(2-2/q)S^2\ge1200(2-2/q)S^3$
is strictly larger than $7(3+1/q)S$ already at $q=18/17$, $S=3$.
Thus the matrix has rank four under these hypotheses.

Here are complete finite algorithms for the remaining table entries.
Write $\omega^2-\tau\omega+\nu=0$, where $\tau\in\{0,1\}$,
and let $\Delta=4\nu-\tau^2$. The identity
\[
 4N(u+v\omega)=(2u+\tau v)^2+\Delta v^2
\]
enumerates the closed norm ball $N(z)\le M$ by
\[
 |v|\le\lfloor\sqrt{4M/\Delta}\rfloor,\qquad
 |2u+\tau v|\le\lfloor\sqrt{4M-\Delta v^2}\rfloor.
\]
All roots, including zero, are retained. For each of the forty pairs
in Table~\ref{tab:pr-forty-pairs}, enumerate $N(r)\le23$ and form
$s=\overline a(r^2-1)/a_0$ whenever both coordinates of the numerator
are divisible by $a_0$. Retain precisely those $s$ distinct from $a,b$
with $b_0\le N(s)\le224$ and $bs+1$ a square.
Completeness follows from $N(r)=|as+1|<15\sqrt2+1<23$.
The resulting fifty-seven triples include $(1,-3,3)$, excluded by
Lemma~\ref{lem:pr-one-three}. The other fifty-six are listed below.

For each retained triple, enumerate $N(r)\le284$ and form
$t=\overline a(r^2-1)/a_0$ with the same coordinate divisibility test.
Retain precisely $t\notin\{a,b,s\}$ with $s_0\le N(t)\le40000$
for which $bt+1$ and $st+1$ are squares.
This is complete for $|t|\le200$, because
$N(r)=|at+1|\le200\sqrt2+1<284$.
All square tests can be made by constructing the set of squares of
roots of norm at most $3001$. Indeed, every tested target has
modulus at most $|st|+1<3001$. Ring operations are exactly
\[
 (u,v)(u',v')=(uu'-\nu vv',\ uv'+u'v+\tau vv'),\qquad
 \overline{(u,v)}=(u+\tau v,-v).
\]
These finite loops specify the search including all boundary cases.
The last column lists every resulting fourth norm with its multiplicity.
A dash denotes an empty set. In each row there is at most one fourth entry with norm at most $40000$. Every listed norm is at least the corresponding
$N_0$, whereas every $N_0\le21270<40000$.
Thus the finite complement $N(t)<N_0$ is empty in every case.
edits.new:
The fifty-six triples in Table~\ref{tab:fixed56} were enumerated at the
end of Section~\ref{sec:pair-reduction}. We now exclude $N(t)<N_0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-irregular} gives $T>2BS$. In thirty-eight rows,
$4b_0s_0\ge N_0$, so this already contradicts $N(t)<N_0$.

For the other rows, put
\[
 q=b+s,\qquad h=1+2bs,\qquad \delta=(b-s)^2-4,
\]
and define
\[
 f(X)=X^2-2(|h|-|q|)X+|\delta|+2|q|+1.
\]
The triple $(b,s,t)$ is irregular by Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-irregular},
so \eqref{eq:irregular-quadratic} gives $f(T)\ge0$.
This quadratic is convex. For $X\ge0$, the bounds
$|h|\ge2BS-1$, $|q|\le B+S$ and
$|\delta|\le(B+S)^2+4$ give
\[
 f(X)\le(B+S+X+1)^2+4-4BSX.
\]
The endpoint calculation in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:irregular-growth} therefore gives $f(2BS)<0$.

For sixteen of the remaining rows, substitution of the displayed
entries and $N_0$ gives $f(\sqrt{N_0})<-100$. These are exact checks
using the rational enclosures defined above. Explicitly,
$[N(h)]_--[N(q)]_+>0$, and
\[
 \begin{split}
 f(\sqrt{N_0})\le{}&N_0
 -2\bigl([N(h)]_--[N(q)]_+\bigr)[N_0]_-\\
 &+[N(\delta)]_++2[N(q)]_++1<-100.
 \end{split}
\]
Convexity excludes $2BS<T<\sqrt{N_0}$ in each of these rows.

The two remaining triples are
$(a,b,s)=(1,-3,-2\pm2\sqrt{-2})$, both with $N_0=1024$.
Here $N(q)=33$, $N(h)=457$ and $N(\delta)=153$, so
\[
 f(30)=901-60\sqrt{457}+62\sqrt{33}+\sqrt{153}<-5.
\]
Use $\sqrt{457}>213/10$, $\sqrt{33}<29/5$ and
$\sqrt{153}<62/5$. Convexity gives $T>30$.
Write $t+1=(u+v\sqrt{-2})^2$ with $u,v\in\mathbb Z$.
If $30<T<32$, then
\[
 29<|t+1|=u^2+2v^2<33.
\]
The values $30$ and $31$ are impossible modulo $16$.
For $u^2+2v^2=32$, reduction modulo $16$ forces $4\mid u,v$,
and then $u=0$, $v=\pm4$. This gives $t=-33$, contrary to $T<32$.
Thus $N(t)<N_0$ is impossible in the last two rows as well.

edits.old: \section{Exclusion when every entry has modulus at least three}

Extensions of $\{1,3\}$ in
$\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-d}]$ were studied by Franu\v{s}i\'c~\cite{F10} and
Kreso and Franu\v{s}i\'c~\cite{FK11}. Here this pair is covered by the
same approximation estimates as the other pairs. We do not determine
whether the bound of five is attained.
edits.new:
Franu\v{s}i\'c~\cite[Theorem~1]{F10} proved that
$\{1,3\}$ cannot be extended to a Diophantine quintuple in
$\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-d}]$ for positive squarefree $d\ne2$.
Franu\v{s}i\'c and Kreso~\cite[Corollary~1.2]{FK11} treated $d=2$.
For $d\equiv3\pmod4$, this subring is properly contained in
$\mathcal O_K$. We handle the pair in the full ring of integers using
the same approximation estimates as for the other pairs. We do not
determine whether the bound of five is attained.
